'''''Juniperus macrocarpa''''' ('''large-fruited juniper''', syn. ''J. oxycedrus'' subsp. ''macrocarpa'' (Sibth. & Sm.) Ball) is a species of [[juniper]], native across the northern [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean Region]] from southwestern [[Spain]]<ref name="Muñoz-Reinoso, 2004">{{cite journal|last=Muñoz-Reinoso|first=José Carlos|title=Diversity of maritime juniper woodlands|journal=Forest Ecology and Management|date=6 May 2004|volume=192|issue=2–3|pages=267–276|doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2004.01.039|bibcode=2004ForEM.192..267M }}<!--|access-date=11 April 2013--></ref> east to western [[Turkey]] and [[Cyprus]], growing on [[coast]]al [[sand dune]]s from sea level up to {{Convert|75|m|abbr=off}} in altitude.<ref name=adams>Adams, R. P. (2004). ''Junipers of the World''. Trafford. {{ISBN|1-4120-4250-X}}</ref><ref name=farjon>Farjon, A. (2005). ''Monograph of Cupressaceae and Sciadopitys''. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. {{ISBN|1-84246-068-4}}</ref> A single, isolated tree is found further west, in a cliff in southern [[Portugal]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sánchez-Gullon |first1=E. |last2=Javier Nieva |first2=F. |last3=Muñoz Rodríguez |first3=A.F. |title=El enebro costero, novedad para Portugal |journal=Conservación Vegetal |date=2015 |volume=19 |page=4 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/280525886}}</ref>
[[Image:Juniperus macrocarpa Paros1.jpg|left|thumb|Foliage and immature cones, Paros Island, Greece]]
It is a spreading [[shrub]] {{Convert|2–5|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} tall, rarely a small [[tree]] up to {{Convert|14|m|abbr=on}} tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are broad lanceolate, produced in whorls of three, green, {{Convert|12–20|mm|frac=4}} long and 2–3 mm broad, with a double white [[stoma]]tal band split by a green midrib on the inner surface. It is [[dioecious]], with separate male and female plants. The [[conifer cone|seed cones]] are [[Juniper berry|berry-like]], green ripening in 18 months to orange-red with a variable pink waxy coating; they are spherical, 12–18 mm diameter, and have six fused scales in two whorls, three of the scales with a single [[seed]]. The seeds are dispersed when [[bird]]s eat the cones, digesting the fleshy scales and passing the hard seeds in their droppings. The [[pollen]] cones are yellow, 2–3 mm long, and fall soon after shedding their pollen in late winter.<ref name=adams/><ref name=farjon/><ref>Arboretum de Villardebelle: [http://www.pinetum.org/cones/JUcones.htm photos of cones and shoots]</ref>

Despite its distinct morphology with large cones and broad leaves more like those of ''[[Juniperus drupacea]]'', it has often been treated as a [[subspecies]] of ''[[Juniperus oxycedrus]]'',<ref name=farjon/> though recent genetic studies<ref name=adams/><ref name=adams1>Adams, R. P. (2000). Systematics of ''Juniperus'' section ''Juniperus'' based on leaf essential oils and RAPD DNA fingerprinting. ''Biochem. Syst. Ecol''. 28: 515-528. [http://www.juniperus.org/AdamsPapersPDFFiles/160-2000bBIOCH28515.pdf available online (pdf file)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721171830/http://www.juniperus.org/AdamsPapersPDFFiles/160-2000bBIOCH28515.pdf |date=2011-07-21 }}</ref><ref name=adams2>Adams, R. P., Morris, J. A., Pandey, R. N., & Schwarzbach, A. E. (2005). Cryptic speciation between ''Juniperus deltoides'' and ''J. oxycedrus'' (Cupressaceae) in the Mediterranean. ''Biochem. Syst. Ecol''. 33: 771-787. [http://www.juniperus.org/AdamsPapersPDFFiles/182-2005BSE33-771.pdf available online (pdf file)]</ref> have shown its [[DNA]] is distinct from that of ''J. oxycedrus''.
